name: complexity_extremity_uniqueness_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers evaluate referents through their complexity extremity (squared deviation from the display's mean feature count, favoring both minimal/empty and maximal/full feature profiles over intermediate items) and contextual uniqueness (inverse duplicate count in the scene). On silent prior trials, choices follow this extremity-and-uniqueness salience directly, whereas on heard-word trials a depth-2 pragmatic listener integrates this prior when inverting a speaker whose simulated depth-1 listener operates on unbiased truth-conditional semantics.

name: perceptual_isolation_l2
detail: contract: candidate.py on 4-object contexts at params {alpha=2.73, w_contrast=-2.44}: the gradient with respect to alpha, w_contrast is not finite (NUTS cannot sample it). Common causes: log(0) — add EPS inside the log; a distribution whose weights are all zero for some value (0/0)
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers reason recursively at depth 2 with common knowledge of an object prior rooted in perceptual isolation: each object's salience is determined by its minimum feature distance to any other object in the display, strongly penalizing identical clones (distance zero) while favoring perceptually isolated items at the extremes of feature space. Unlike the incumbent depth-1 confusion model or the 6-parameter additive feature-weight model, this single isolation prior enters at depth-1 and depth-2 speaker planning while the literal listener remains purely truth-conditional, sharply diverging on multi-step disambiguation displays with clones and extreme-feature objects (such as a 4-object display with a plain singleton, two intermediate objects, and a maximally complex object) where isolation captures both clone avoidance and prior extremity preference with just two parameters.

name: extension_confusion_cost_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Pragmatic listeners reason at depth 2 about a speaker who chooses words to maximize communicative informativeness while avoiding expressions whose alternative referents are perceptually redundant or confusable. Specifically, speakers incur an expected referential confusion cost proportional to the average visual feature similarity among the objects in a word's extension and the target, while listeners expect speakers to refer to perceptually isolated targets whose feature complexity deviates sharply from the scene average (especially sparse objects).

name: competitor_confusion_shared_prior
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Refining competitor_confusion_speaker by incorporating the baseline competitor-confusion object prior into the simulated speaker's referent prior in depth-1 listener reasoning, replacing the uniform referent prior while keeping the literal listener, recursion depth, the two parameters (rationality and confusion aversion), and the speaker's confusion penalty unchanged. When listeners and speakers share common knowledge that visually confusable or duplicate objects are less likely intended referents a priori, listeners not only expect speakers to avoid words shared with confusable competitors, but also weight visually distinct non-clone referents higher when inverting the speaker's utterance choice. This shared prior explains why listeners strongly favor non-clone valid referents in heard-word scenes with identical clone competitors and avoids over-penalizing valid referents whose alternative features are shared across distinct objects.

name: competitor_confusion_prior_l1
detail: not novel: its listener and speaker predictions are within RMSE 0.0000 of competitor_confusion_shared_prior's (threshold 0.002) over the novelty pool of 1597 scenes. A re-parameterisation of an existing mechanism is not a new hypothesis; change what the listener or speaker computes.
hypothesis: Pragmatic listeners at recursion depth one invert a competitor-confusion-averse speaker under a common-knowledge baseline confusion prior that favors visually distinct referents over confusable distractors and identical clones. Refining competitor_confusion_speaker with no parameters added or removed (keeping only alpha and w_confusion), the same depth-one L1 calling literal L0, and the identical compute_confusion_and_prior calculation, the sole change is replacing the uniform referent prior inside L1 with the baseline confusion prior already computed for silent prior trials. Because identical clones share every feature, their mutual similarity cancels out across candidate words in the speaker's utterance softmax (and has no effect when a clone has only one true word), so integrating the baseline confusion prior into L1 explains why listeners in exp1 and E select non-clone valid referents over identical clones when hearing a shared word.

name: competitor_confusion_l2
detail: admitted

name: crowding_impurity_prior_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers share a pre-linguistic expectation over referents governed by perceptual crowding and internal feature impurity: before hearing any word, people penalize objects by their summed similarity to other display items and by the internal variance across their present and absent scene features. Because empty and maximally complex objects have zero internal feature variance while single-feature objects have lower variance than mixed intermediate objects, this prior explains why people strongly favor empty, minimal, and maximal referents over intermediate ones on silent prior trials while avoiding crowded clones. At recursion depth 2, the pragmatic listener inverts a speaker who plans for a depth-1 listener under this shared object prior, grounded in a purely truth-conditional literal listener.

name: attentional_load_l1
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Listeners interpret referring expressions under limited visual attention to the display's feature matrix: an object's baseline visual salience reflects how strongly its feature density stands out from the scene average (favoring sparse minimal objects and full-featured objects over intermediate ones) while penalizing visually confusable neighbors. On heard-word trials, a depth-one pragmatic listener inverts a confusion-averse speaker under this shared salience prior, but when a heard word's extension spans most of the display while still leaving a false distractor, attentional overload in feature verification causes the listener's posterior to partially fall back toward the baseline visual salience prior.

name: noisy_graded_semantics_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers communicate under soft, noisy lexical semantics (graded truth values diluted across an object's features, with baseline semantic confusion across features and objects) and a single perceptual salience prior combining contextual uniqueness, feature distinctiveness, and relative complexity extremity. Because word applicability is diluted on feature-dense objects and non-zero semantic noise allows false objects to compete, listeners assign higher false-alarm weight when a word's extension is diluted across three valid referents than when it picks out two, while favoring sparse or extreme singletons on silent and ambiguous trials.

name: complexity_scaled_competitor_confusion
detail: contract: candidate.py's speaker on 4-object scenes: the gradient with respect to alpha, w_confusion is not finite
hypothesis: Refining `competitor_confusion_shared_prior` with no parameters added or removed (retaining only `alpha` and `w_confusion`) and the same recursion depth (`L1` calling literal `L0`), by scaling pairwise visual similarity in `compute_confusion_and_prior` by the objects' feature counts: replacing `sim = jnp.exp(-dist) * (1.0 - eye)` with `sim = jnp.exp(-dist) * (1.0 - eye) * (ctx.feature_count[:, None] + ctx.feature_count[None, :])`, while keeping all other terms (`feats`, `dist`, `real_words`, `real_lex`, `confusion = real_lex @ sim`, `baseline_confusion = jnp.sum(sim, axis=1)`, `prior = softmax_prior(-w_confusion * baseline_confusion)`, `L0`, `L1`, and `listener`) unchanged. Psychologically, perceptual crowding and referential confusion between two objects grow with the number of visual features they display, whereas sparse objects (zero-feature empty objects and minimal single-feature objects) induce far less visual crowding with their neighbors even at small Hamming distances. Scaling pairwise confusion by feature complexity explains why listeners on silent prior trials strongly favor empty zero-feature and minimal single-feature objects over intermediate multi-feature objects, and why on heard-word trials listeners favor simpler valid referents and 1- or 2-feature clones over complex 3-feature competitors without adding any free parameters.

name: competitor_confusion_extremity_prior
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Refining competitor_confusion_shared_prior by incorporating the relative feature-complexity extremity prior component from extension_confusion_cost_l2 into the shared baseline object prior, adding one parameter (w_extremity) while keeping the literal listener L0, depth-1 listener L1, the rationality and confusion-aversion parameters (alpha and w_confusion), and the speaker's competitor-confusion penalty unchanged. Listeners and speakers share common knowledge that speakers are less likely to refer to visually confusable or duplicate objects and more likely to refer to objects whose feature complexity deviates sharply from the scene average, especially minimal zero-feature and single-feature items. Adding this relative complexity-extremity term to the shared prior explains why listeners on silent prior trials strongly favor empty zero-feature objects and minimal single-feature objects over intermediate two- and three-feature objects, and why listeners on ambiguous heard-word trials favor simpler valid referents across E and exp1.

name: competitor_confusion_extremity_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Refining competitor_confusion_l2 by incorporating the relative feature-complexity extremity component from extension_confusion_cost_l2 into the shared object prior, adding one parameter (w_extremity) while keeping recursion depth at two (L2 calling L1, which calls literal L0), the parameters alpha and w_confusion, and the speaker's pairwise similarity confusion penalty at both speaker levels unchanged. Listeners and speakers share common knowledge of an object prior that penalizes visually confusable or duplicate objects while favoring objects whose feature complexity deviates sharply from the scene average, especially empty zero-feature and minimal single-feature items relative to intermediate two- or three-feature items. Combining relative complexity extremity with the shared baseline confusion prior in depth-two competitor-confusion reasoning explains why listeners strongly favor empty and minimal single-feature objects on silent prior trials as well as simpler valid referents and multi-feature referents with unique alternative features on ambiguous heard-word trials across E and exp1.

name: diagnostic_contrast_heuristic
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers interpret and select words through a non-Bayesian diagnostic contrast heuristic rather than recursive Theory of Mind: each feature's diagnosticity combines its direct specificity (inversely proportional to the number of objects possessing it) and its effective specificity across objects weighted by their reliance on that feature, while each object's perceptual anchor salience combines contextual singleton pop-out, pairwise feature distinctiveness, and complexity extremity (penalizing intermediate feature counts between the scene's minimum and maximum). When a word is heard, the listener scores each object in a single step by its noisy feature match (diluted by the object's feature count and the word's effective competition, with false-alarm leakage growing with the word's extension share) minus the diagnosticity of all unmentioned features the object possesses, weighted by the object's perceptual anchor salience. On silent trials without an informative word, listeners choose directly from the perceptual anchor distribution.

name: uncertainty_gated_belief_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers infer referents by probability matching over a capacity-bounded belief distribution where pragmatic reasoning is gated by an utterance's referential uncertainty (the ratio of competing true referents to scene objects) and anchored by a boundary-extremity visual prior. When a word's extension spans most of the display while leaving a false distractor, high referential uncertainty causes the listener's decision rule to partially fall back from depth-two pragmatic beliefs toward the visual boundary-extremity prior, explaining elevated false alarms on three-true displays and strong avoidance of intermediate-complexity objects on silent trials across E and exp1.

name: contrastive_aspect_qud_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Speakers and listeners organize reference around a Question Under Discussion (QUD) about how a referent's visual aspect contrasts with the display: before hearing a word, listeners expect the topic to be an object whose feature profile stands out through Weber-scaled complexity extremity, contextual uniqueness, and complexity-normalized feature distinctiveness (explaining why silent trials in E and exp1 favor minimal and maximal complexity outliers over intermediate objects). When a word is uttered, it addresses a feature-dimension QUD whose positive aspect applicability is moderated by the referent's normalized unmentioned feature load and feature overlap with competitors in the word's extension (explaining why listeners in E and exp1 select multi-feature referents whose unmentioned features do not overlap with the word's competitors on two-referent and four-referent trials), while an over-general word that applies to most of the scene also activates the complement QUD partition cell in proportion to its positive extension share and complement specificity (explaining false-alarm choices and ratings when a word is true of three of four objects).

name: extension_noisy_graded_semantics_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Refining noisy_graded_semantics_l2 with no parameters added or removed (retaining only alpha and w_salience) and the same recursion depth (L2 calling L1, which calls L0), by scaling each real word's semantic confusion noise on false objects by the squared proportion of display objects in that word's literal extension: defining ext_size = jnp.sum(real_lex, axis=1, keepdims=True) and replacing sem_noise = 1.0 / (n_utt * n_obj) with sem_noise = (ext_size * ext_size) / (n_utt * n_obj * n_obj), while keeping all other terms (real_mask, real_lex, diff, pair_dist, is_singleton, distinct, n_real, fc_norm, fc_dev, extremity, prior, fc_safe, graded_true, noisy_real, soft_lex, L0, L1, L2, listener, and speaker) unchanged. Under uniform constant noise across utterances, depth-two pragmatic recursion suppresses false-alarm probabilities on three-of-four valid-referent trials to nearly zero because two levels of speaker likelihood inversion amplify the ratio between valid and false referents. Because a word that spans most of the display induces greater referential crowding and feature-verification interference across objects than a word with a small extension, scaling semantic confusion by the squared extension proportion explains why listeners make substantially more false-alarm choices when a heard word applies to three of four objects than when it applies to two across E and exp1.

name: noisy_graded_semantics_extremity_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Refining noisy_graded_semantics_l2 by incorporating the relative feature-complexity extremity weight (w_extremity) from competitor_confusion_extremity_l2 to decouple complexity extremity from singleton-and-distinctiveness salience in the shared object prior, while keeping recursion depth at two (L2 calling L1, which calls L0), the soft noisy lexical semantics (soft_lex), and the speaker definition unchanged. Specifically, PARAMS adds w_extremity with prior Normal(0.0, 1.0) alongside alpha and w_salience, and compute_soft_lex_and_prior replaces softmax_prior(w_salience * (is_singleton + distinct + extremity)) with softmax_prior(w_salience * (is_singleton + distinct) + w_extremity * extremity). Because contextual uniqueness and distinctiveness have larger magnitudes than normalized complexity extremity, tying all three terms to a single scalar weight under-weights complexity extremity, whereas separating w_extremity allows listeners on silent prior trials and ambiguous four-true trials to strongly favor minimal-complexity referents and avoid intermediate-complexity referents across E and exp1.

name: attentional_load_l2
detail: admitted
hypothesis: Refining `attentional_load_l1` by increasing the pragmatic recursion depth from depth 1 (`L1` calling literal `L0`) to depth 2 (`L2` calling `L1`, which calls literal `L0`, with the speaker at both levels using `prior` and penalizing utterances by `w_confusion * at(confusion, u, r)`), with no parameters added or removed (retaining only `alpha` and `w_confusion`) and keeping `L0`, `L1`, `compute_attention_and_prior`, and the top-level attentional overload fallback in `listener` unchanged. Listeners interpret referring expressions by inverting a depth-two speaker who plans for a depth-one pragmatic listener under a shared salience prior favoring complexity-extremity outliers and visually isolated referents, while high-extension heard words that leave a false distractor trigger attentional overload and partially fall back toward the baseline visual salience prior. Extending recursion to depth 2 explains how listeners resolve twice-implicated referents and shared-versus-unique alternative features on multi-feature displays in E and exp1 while preserving the false-alarm and silent-prior predictions of capacity-bounded attentional allocation.

detail: ineligible: more than 4 SEs behind the best on E: 1761.5 ± 255.7
hypothesis: Perceptual oddity heuristic listener. Listeners interpret referring expressions using a perceptual oddity heuristic rather than recursive Theory of Mind. On uninformative trials without an informative word, listeners spontaneously choose the unique singleton, defaulting to uniform choice when all items are distinct or no oddity contrast exists. A lapse parameter captures random clicking.

name: rsa_l2
detail: ineligible: more than 4 SEs behind the best on E: 554.5 ± 132.5
hypothesis: RSA pragmatic listener at depth 2, uniform prior over objects. Depth-2 reasoning is what the pragmods "complex" game needs to single out the object described by the twice-implicated word. One rationality alpha at every level; uniform choice with no informative word; a lapse parameter mixes in uniform guessing.

name: rsa_l1

With no informative word the choice is uniform. A lapse parameter mixes in uniform guessing.

hypothesis: Refining extension_noisy_graded_semantics_l2 by removing the extension-scaled semantic confusion noise on literally false objects so that lexical semantics is strictly truth-conditional graded applicability (`soft_lex = graded_true = ctx.lex / fc_safe`), with no parameters added or removed (retaining only `alpha` and `w_salience`), the same recursion depth (`L2` calling `L1`, which calls `L0`), and all other terms (`real_mask`, `real_lex`, `diff`, `pair_dist`, `is_singleton`, `distinct`, `n_real`, `fc_norm`, `fc_dev`, `extremity`, `prior`, `fc_safe`, `graded_true`, `L0`, `L1`, `L2`, `listener`, and `speaker`) unchanged (removing `n_utt`, `n_obj`, `ext_size`, `sem_noise`, and `noisy_real`). Assigning positive semantic weight to literally false referents causes tempered listener probabilities on rating paradigms (exp2) to inflate false-referent ratings and compress the contrast between maximal-feature valid referents and literally false referents, whereas truth-conditional graded semantics leaves rare false-referent responses to the paradigm link's lapse while preserving graded feature dilution across valid referents.

name: cooccurrence_lexical_uncertainty_l2
detail: ineligible: more than 4 SEs behind the best on exp1: 93.0 ± 19.2
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers communicate under lexical uncertainty in which a word's meaning is softened across the visual features that co-occur on the objects in its literal extension: each word primarily activates its canonical feature (diluted by the object's feature load) but, when referentially ambiguous, also partially activates co-occurring features shared by its valid referents. This co-occurrence lexical uncertainty boosts multi-feature valid referents on broad and universal utterances while restricting false-alarm leakage strictly to distractors that share co-occurring features with the word's extension, under a perceptual salience prior where verifying an empty object requires scanning all scene features.

name: feature_rich_l1_graded_l2

hypothesis: Refining `l1_graded_semantics_l2` with no parameters added or removed (retaining only `alpha` and `w_salience`) and the same recursion depth (`L2` calling `L1`, which calls `L0`), by adding normalized feature richness `fc_norm` to the object salience prior so that `prior = softmax_prior(w_salience * (is_singleton + distinct + extremity + fc_norm))` instead of `softmax_prior(w_salience * (is_singleton + distinct + extremity))`, while keeping all other terms (`real_mask`, `real_lex`, `diff`, `pair_dist`, `is_singleton`, `distinct`, `n_real`, `fc_norm`, `fc_dev`, `extremity`, `n_utt`, `n_obj`, `ext_size`, `sem_noise`, `fc_safe`, `graded_true`, `noisy_real`, `soft_lex`, `L0`, `L1`, `L2`, `listener`, and `speaker`) unchanged. In `l1_graded_semantics_l2`, dividing `fc_dev * fc_dev` by `fc_norm + 1.0 / n_real` in `extremity` makes 0-feature objects more salient than featureful objects on prior trials and penalizes the highest-feature-count object when an uninformative word applies to every object in the display; including `fc_norm` in the shared salience prior balances the 0-feature denominator advantage with a positive preference for feature-rich referents, explaining why listeners rate featureful objects above 0-feature objects on silent prior trials and give substantially higher ratings to the maximal-feature object on uninformative all-true word trials in exp2.

name: richness_grounded_salience_l2_2
detail: ineligible: more than 4 SEs behind the best on E: 216.9 ± 53.8, exp1: 122.6 ± 30.0
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers share a perceptual salience prior over referents that combines contextual singleton uniqueness, pairwise feature distinctiveness, and complexity extremity, while the literal listener grounds word meaning in an object's feature richness and each feature's contextual specificity. At depth one, a speaker with graded, extension-crowded lexical access plans for this richness-grounded literal listener, and at depth two a truth-conditional speaker plans for the depth-one pragmatic listener under the shared salience prior. Grounding literal interpretation in feature richness and specificity prevents depth-two reasoning from over-penalizing complex valid referents on uninformative and ambiguous utterances while preserving singleton and extremity preferences across choice and rating paradigms.

name: truth_conditional_diagnostic_contrast
detail: ineligible: more than 4 SEs behind the best on E: 343.4 ± 67.9, exp1: 148.3 ± 28.2
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers interpret and select words through a non-Bayesian diagnostic contrast heuristic rather than recursive Theory of Mind: each feature's diagnosticity combines its direct specificity (inversely proportional to the number of objects possessing it) and its effective specificity across objects weighted by their reliance on that feature, while each object's perceptual anchor salience combines contextual singleton pop-out, pairwise feature distinctiveness, and complexity extremity (where verifying an empty object requires scanning all scene features). When a word is heard, the listener scores each valid referent in a single step by its feature match (diluted by the object's feature count and the word's effective competition) minus the diagnosticity of all unmentioned features the object possesses, anchored by the object's perceptual salience; on silent trials without an informative word, choices follow the perceptual anchor distribution directly.

name: aspect_coverage_qud_l2
detail: ineligible: more than 4 SEs behind the best on exp1: 119.2 ± 29.3
hypothesis: Speakers plan referring expressions under a joint communicative goal that trades off object-identity disambiguation against aspectual feature alignment, evaluating candidate words by how strongly they concentrate listener belief on the target and how diagnostically the target's positive feature profile covers the scene's shared feature structure. Listeners invert this aspect-guided speaker at depth two under a shared perceptual salience prior combining contextual uniqueness, pairwise feature distinctiveness, and non-empty complexity extremity, while over-general utterances that leave a single unmentioned distractor induce contrast-cell leakage only onto feature-bearing competitors that share unmentioned features with the word's extension.

name: l1_availability_graded_l2
detail: ineligible: more than 4 SEs behind the best on exp1: 125.2 ± 28.4
hypothesis: Refining l1_graded_semantics_l2 with no parameters added or removed (retaining only alpha and w_salience) and the same recursion depth (L2 calling L1, which calls L0), by scaling the L1 speaker's true-feature lexical weight by contextual feature availability (ext_size / n_obj) so that graded_true = (ctx.lex * ext_size) / (fc_safe * n_obj), while keeping all other terms (real_mask, real_lex, diff, pair_dist, is_singleton, distinct, n_real, fc_norm, fc_dev, extremity, prior, n_utt, n_obj, ext_size, sem_noise, fc_safe, noisy_real, soft_lex, L0, L1, L2, listener, and speaker) unchanged. In l1_graded_semantics_l2, the L1 speaker weights every true feature of an object equally by 1 / fc_safe regardless of how salient that feature is across the display, causing L1 to under-produce widely shared four-object words relative to narrower two-object words and causing the L2 listener to over-predict the rating drop between two-referent and four-referent valid objects in exp2. Weighting the L1 speaker's true-feature access by scene-wide feature availability (ext_size / n_obj) boosts L1 production of broad four-referent words on multi-feature objects and compresses the L2 listener's probability gap between two-referent and four-referent valid objects, closing the extension-size 2-versus-4 rating discrepancy in exp2 while preserving E and exp1 choice accuracy.

name: uncertainty_gated_belief_l2
detail: elpd_diff 1059.9 > 2.0 x clustered dse 449.5 vs l1_graded_semantics_l2 on exp2 (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners and speakers infer referents by probability matching over a capacity-bounded belief distribution where pragmatic reasoning is gated by an utterance's referential uncertainty (the ratio of competing true referents to scene objects) and anchored by a boundary-extremity visual prior. When a word's extension spans most of the display while leaving a false distractor, high referential uncertainty causes the listener's decision rule to partially fall back from depth-two pragmatic beliefs toward the visual boundary-extremity prior, explaining elevated false alarms on three-true displays and strong avoidance of intermediate-complexity objects on silent trials across E and exp1.

name: truth_gated_uncertainty_belief_l2
detail: elpd_diff 784.3 > 2.0 x clustered dse 390.0 vs l1_graded_semantics_l2 on exp2 (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Refining uncertainty_gated_belief_l2 with no parameters added or removed (retaining only alpha and w_salience), the same recursion depth (L2 calling L1, which calls L0), and the same compute_lex_prior_and_gate helper, by replacing the L2 speaker's noisy lexical filter at(lex, u, r) with the literal truth-conditional indicator (at(lex, u, r) > sem_noise) inside L2 (passing sem_noise into L2 and leaving L0, L1, prior, gate, listener, and speaker unchanged). When speakers restrict top-level production strictly to literally true utterances while simulating a depth-one listener with noisy graded verification, literally false referents receive zero speaker likelihood at L2 and only receive non-zero listener probability when high referential uncertainty triggers the prior fallback gate (such as three-of-four extension trials), preventing false-referent probability inflation on one- and two-referent trials in exp2 while preserving false-alarm and extremity predictions across E and exp1.
